a66f680195: The voice you were born with
36bcfbc476: A breathy sound leaks more air, a nasal sound keeps the resonance in the nose, and a full sound balances all three resonating spaces. Use the same voice a different way and you get a different tone. Lessons 2 and 3 practise each one.

e7bc1b4d76: Build① The basics of how sound is made
a8a2e76979: Vibration can be big or small, fast or slow, long or short
3ca613b915: Sets the volume: the more force the breath puts on the vocal folds, the bigger the amplitude.
440ec5f0a0: Sets the pitch: A4 = 440 Hz, and an octave higher is 880 Hz.
c3043daa23: Inversely related to frequency: low notes travel further, which is why the neighbours always hear the bass first.
2af2431717: Build② The basics of how sound is amplified
2eb9988560:
1. Pluck the open strings in order from the sixth to the first.
2. Do it again, stopping each string with your right hand straight after plucking.
3. Press all the strings at the 12th fret with your left index finger and pluck again.
4. Repeat experiment 1 while facing a wall, moving from far to near.

Now try it with your voice: hum the same note in the middle of the room and in a corner, and write down the difference.

79d1067329: Tempo and rhythm: rushing or dragging both make a song lose its centre.
d3b3ef7d2f: Rhythm challenge: listen to the demo first, then after the four-beat count-in, sing the same rhythm on "Ta". Orange marks are the target beats, triangles are the beats you sang, and they turn green when you hit. Start with quarter notes, then work up to syncopation and offbeats.
a96b3021d5: Build③ What listeners hear｜Teacher demo
4aca9bfff5: Teacher demo: Bruno Mars, "I Just Might"
78e81cfa42: Style in brief｜Retro disco pop blended with funk and soul
f1eed50122: Released in January 2026, it went straight to number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in its first week. Short syncopated electric guitar, a bouncing bass, a horn section of sax, trumpet and trombone, and handclaps drive a mid-tempo groove of about 103 beats per minute.
f055acb6ff: In the repeated chorus line "I just might", notice whether it lands on the same pitch every time. The busier the backing, the more the voice needs to lock onto the chords.
7e69432c6c: Compare verse and chorus: which part stays close and speech-like, and which opens up and gets brighter? Notice how the voice matches the brightness of the horns and guitar.
97364dc88e: Funk lyrics often land on offbeats and syncopations. Tap along on "Tap tempo" to check it's about 103, then notice when the voice jumps ahead of the beat and when it lands right on it.

45b737c6e6: A question for guitarists: the strumming and fingerpicking patterns you play belong mainly to which element?
ef9b2ee7c2: Strumming and fingerpicking patterns set the song's groove, so they belong to rhythm; the chords your left hand presses belong to harmony. The pie chart in the original notes spelled them "Hamonic" and "Rythem"; the correct spellings are Harmony and Rhythm.

61f5441fad: Challenge: arrange the eight sections in the order they first appear in a song.
56575336d2: Intro → Verse → Pre-chorus → Chorus → after the interlude, back to the verse → after the second chorus comes the bridge → back to the chorus → Outro → Ending. A tag often appears in the last chorus, and not every song has a pre-chorus or bridge.
b61e8c0cd2: TurnThe role of each section

4d889a68ac: Tell the story in a mid-to-low rangeClose to a speaking voice, holding back about 30% of the volume.
50d8c0def1: Push the emotion upwardGradually use more air, building energy for the chorus.
9a895d643f: The song's centre and its hookThe fullest resonance and strongest emotion, usually the highest note too.
373bdc0d6e: A rest for the singerReset your breath and get ready for round two.
3c518b2f88: A turn in melody or moodChange tone or intensity so the last chorus hits harder.
1ee6b6e288: Repeat or extend the last lineYou can change the rhythm or slow down to let it linger.
